material-handling.name: Material Handling
material-handling.label: Constructive
material-handling.summary: Automation demand remains supported by labor pressure, resilience planning and service expectations, while financing, tariffs and integration risk keep investment disciplined.
brief: The material handling and warehouse automation market is entering a more favorable period after several years of normalization and delayed capital decisions. The underlying need for automation remains strong because customers continue to face labor constraints, fulfillment complexity and pressure to build more resilient supply chains.

Competitive advantage is shifting from installing individual technologies toward integrating complete operating systems. Customers increasingly expect conveyors, AS/RS, robotics, AMRs, controls, safety and warehouse software to work together with common diagnostics, useful data and a credible lifecycle model.

The strongest near-term opportunities are scalable brownfield modernization, connected material-flow systems, robotics that address labor and safety constraints, and lifecycle services that address obsolescence and cybersecurity.
leaders: Orchestrating mixed fleets and automation technologies

outlook.text: Disciplined investment continues in projects with clear throughput, labor, reliability and service-level outcomes.
Lower financing friction, reshoring and stronger logistics activity accelerate greenfield and multi-site programs.
Tariff or financial volatility delays large projects while retrofit, service and productivity work remains active.

material-handling.economics: Manufacturing expansion, reshoring and renewed warehouse investment support demand. Elevated input costs, financing conditions and tariffs keep customers focused on measurable throughput, labor, space and uptime outcomes.

process.name: Process
process.label: Constructive
process.summary: Secure, phased modernization is supported by reliability, cybersecurity and workforce priorities, while brownfield complexity keeps investment disciplined.
brief: Process industries continue to face a compelling modernization need driven by aging controls, cybersecurity exposure, limited engineering resources and the loss of experienced operators.

Industrial AI and analytics gain credibility when grounded in process context and integrated into existing work practices. Interoperability and secure connectivity enable phased modernization rather than disruptive replacement.
The strongest opportunities are secure control migration, connected asset performance, energy optimization, operator enablement and standardized skid architectures.
leaders: Modernizing brownfield systems without disrupting production
Preserving operator knowledge and process expertise

outlook.text: Phased modernization continues around reliability, security and lifecycle risk.
Improved confidence accelerates control migration and connected asset programs.
Capacity projects slow while compliance and reliability work continues.

process.economics: Industrial expansion supports process demand, but energy, regulatory requirements, input costs and brownfield execution risk favor phased programs with measurable reliability outcomes.

heavy-industries.name: Heavy Industries
heavy-industries.label: Constructive
heavy-industries.summary: Critical-material demand supports long-term investment, while commodity volatility and project complexity favor reliability and selective brownfield work.
brief: Heavy industries benefit from durable demand drivers tied to infrastructure, electrification and regional supply security, but commodity cycles and high capital intensity make the market selective.
Operators emphasize reliability, debottlenecking, safety and energy performance. Aging assets raise the value of condition monitoring, resilient controls and planned lifecycle modernization.
The strongest positioning combines domain knowledge with robust architectures that remain supportable over long asset lives.
leaders: Protecting returns through selective capital investment
Regional supply security and critical-material demand

outlook.text: Reliability and debottlenecking work outpaces broad capacity expansion.
Critical-material investment and infrastructure accelerate strategic projects.
Commodity weakness delays greenfield work while service remains resilient.

heavy-industries.economics: Commodity prices, energy, permitting and financing strongly influence project timing. Reliability, autonomous operations and outage-based modernization remain comparatively resilient.

manufacturing-assembly.name: Manufacturing & Assembly
manufacturing-assembly.label: Positive
manufacturing-assembly.summary: Manufacturing expansion and workforce pressure support flexible automation, while customers continue to require clear ROI and repeatable integration.
brief: Discrete manufacturers face expanding activity, skill constraints and greater product-mix complexity, supporting robotics, vision, motion and digital production.
Manufacturers increasingly want reusable cells and machine architectures supporting multiple products, faster changeovers and future expansion.
Differentiation comes from making flexibility and repeatability measurable through launch speed, quality, utilization and lifecycle support.
leaders: Flexible automation for greater product variety
Robotics, vision, motion and safety convergence

outlook.text: Flexible automation investment continues around quality and labor outcomes.
Manufacturing expansion accelerates reusable cell and line programs.
Capacity programs slow while quality and productivity projects persist.

manufacturing-assembly.economics: Manufacturing expansion supports automation demand, although input costs reward reusable cells and projects with clear quality, utilization and launch-speed outcomes.

packaging.name: Packaging
packaging.label: Positive
packaging.summary: Packaging machinery demand remains favorable as flexibility, robotics and lifecycle services address SKU complexity, labor pressure and resilience.
brief: Packaging operations must handle more variety, shorter runs, workforce turnover and changing materials while maintaining throughput and quality.
Customers increasingly value mix-adjusted throughput, maintainability and rapid recovery rather than maximum rated speed alone.
Lifecycle value is a larger part of OEM differentiation as obsolescence and knowledge loss create operating risk.

outlook.text: Flexible machinery and lifecycle services support steady growth.
CPG investment accelerates new lines and robotics.
Retrofit and obsolescence work holds up as new lines slow.

packaging.economics: CPG production remains resilient, while SKU proliferation, labor pressure and changing materials support flexible machinery and lifecycle investment.

converting-printing-web.name: Converting, Printing & Web
converting-printing-web.label: Positive
converting-printing-web.summary: Precision automation, inspection and workflow modernization support productivity as shorter runs and substrate complexity reshape economics.
brief: Converting and web operations are adapting to shorter quantities, customization, evolving substrates and pressure to reduce waste.
Small variations in tension, registration, coating weight or winding can create quality losses that compound rapidly.
Digital and conventional workflows are converging across printing, coating, laminating, slitting and finishing.
leaders: New substrates, coatings and roll-to-roll applications

outlook.text: Automation and inspection improve yield and flexibility.
Advanced coatings and new roll-to-roll applications expand demand.
Efficiency and quality investment continues despite slower capacity.

converting-printing-web.economics: Material prices, waste, run length and application mix directly affect margins. Automation improving first-pass yield and setup remains defensible.
